title: NOT EVERY CLOSED DOOR IS THE DEVIL—AND NOT EVERY OPEN DOOR IS GOD.
paragraphs: NOT EVERY CLOSED DOOR IS THE DEVIL—AND NOT EVERY OPEN DOOR IS GOD.

The opportunity you prayed for could become the compromise that destroys you. And the rejection you cried over could be the mercy that protects you. Before you call something a blessing or a spiritual attack, there is a biblical truth your heart desperately needs to understand.
There is a frightening possibility that many Christians never seriously consider.
What if the door you have been begging God to open is the very door He never asked you to walk through?
And what if the door you have been rebuking the devil for closing was never an attack in the first place?
You prayed. You fasted. You waited. You cried yourself to sleep asking God for direction.
Then suddenly, something happened.
A job offer arrived. Someone expressed romantic interest. A business opportunity appeared. A person from your past returned. The money became available. The obstacles disappeared.
And because everything seemed to fall into place, you whispered, "This must be God."
But was it?
Or did you simply assume that because something became possible, it must have become permissible?
Somewhere along the journey of following Jesus, many believers have adopted a dangerous way of interpreting life.
If the door opens, God must be blessing it.
If the door closes, Satan must be fighting it.
If the journey becomes easy, we must be in God's will.
If the journey becomes painful, we must have missed His direction.
But Scripture tells a much more complicated, much more beautiful, and sometimes much more uncomfortable story.
Because ease is not always evidence of God's approval. Resistance is not always evidence of Satan's interference. And success is not always proof of obedience.
You can be moving in the right direction and encounter terrible opposition.
You can be moving in the wrong direction and encounter extraordinary opportunities.
And if your entire understanding of God's guidance depends on whether circumstances cooperate with your desires, you may end up calling temptation a blessing and obedience a mistake.
Listen carefully.
There is a difference between asking God to guide your steps and expecting circumstances to make every decision for you.
And that difference can change your entire life.
The apostle John wrote something that should make every believer more careful about what they accept as spiritual truth.
"Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world." — 1 John 4:1, KJV
In the original Greek, the command includes these words:
μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε, ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα
Mē panti pneumati pisteuete, alla dokimazete ta pneumata.
"Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits."
That word δοκιμάζετε (dokimazete) comes from dokimazō, meaning to test, examine, or evaluate in order to determine what is genuine.

John was specifically warning believers not to accept every spiritual claim or teacher without testing what was being proclaimed. The immediate context concerns false prophets and the confession of Jesus Christ truly come in the flesh.
He was not teaching that every opportunity, inconvenience, or coincidence contains a hidden spiritual message.
But the principle of refusing untested spiritual claims carries an important lesson for discernment.
Just because someone says, "God told me," does not mean God spoke. And just because a circumstance feels significant does not mean you have interpreted it correctly.
Sometimes what needs testing is not the door.
It is the conclusion you have already made about the door.
Because the human heart has an extraordinary ability to find confirmation for something it desperately wants.
We can call impatience "faith."
We can call attraction "divine connection."
We can call financial opportunity "favor."
We can call fear "discernment."
We can even call disobedience "following where God leads."
And the most dangerous part?
We can do all of it while sincerely believing we are honoring Jesus.
Think about Jonah.
God gave Jonah a clear command to go to Nineveh.
Jonah did not want to go.
Instead, he went down to Joppa and found a ship heading toward Tarshish, away from the assignment God had given him.
Scripture says:
"But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish." — Jonah 1:3, KJV
Read that again.
He found a ship.
There was transportation available.
There was a destination that matched his intentions.
There was a way forward.
The opportunity existed.
And yet he was running from God's explicit command.
Imagine Jonah applying the simplistic theology many Christians use today.
"I prayed about it, and there was a ship available. The timing worked. I even had the fare. Surely God opened this door."
But the ship did not turn his rebellion into obedience.
The available passage did not cancel the word God had already spoken.
And the fact that Jonah could afford the journey did not mean he belonged on it.
Sometimes the door is open because the world contains choices.
Sometimes an opportunity exists because another person offered it.
Sometimes circumstances align without providing any divine endorsement of what you intend to do.
And sometimes the fact that you can do something has absolutely nothing to do with whether you should.
That truth becomes painfully personal when you think about relationships.
Someone enters your life.
They know exactly what to say.
They make you feel seen after years of being overlooked.
They give you attention when you have been starving for affection.
And you begin telling yourself that God must have sent them because you prayed for companionship.
But slowly, things begin changing.
Your convictions become negotiable.
Your boundaries become inconvenient.
Your prayer life grows quieter.
You start hiding conversations.
You find yourself defending behaviors that you once knew were wrong.
Yet you keep saying, "But God opened this door."
Beloved, a relationship does not become holy simply because it arrived after a prayer.
And attention does not become love merely because loneliness made it feel like rescue.
The question is not simply whether someone entered your life.
The question is whether the relationship is consistent with the truth and character of Christ.
Because God will not contradict His revealed moral will in order to fulfill your emotional desires.
But now consider the opposite danger.
What happens when a door closes?
What happens when you obey God, do what is right, and still lose something?
What happens when the application gets rejected, the relationship ends, the business struggles, or the people you trusted walk away?
Many believers immediately assume they are under spiritual attack.
They begin rebuking everything.
They blame the devil for every delay.
They interpret every disappointment as proof that some invisible enemy is blocking their destiny.
But Scripture does not permit us to make that conclusion automatically.
Consider the apostle Paul.
In Acts 16:6–7, Paul and his companions were prevented from preaching in certain regions. The passage explicitly attributes those restrictions to the Holy Spirit and the Spirit of Jesus.
They were not trying to commit some obvious sin.
They were seeking to carry the Gospel.
Yet their intended route was blocked.
Later, Paul received a vision directing the mission toward Macedonia.
The closed routes were part of God's guidance in that particular biblical account.
But notice something important.
The text identifies God's involvement because Scripture reveals it—not because Paul taught us that every blocked plan must be a supernatural prohibition.
That distinction matters.
We must not take a specific event in biblical history and turn it into an infallible formula for interpreting every inconvenience in our lives.
A closed door may involve God's providential restraint.
It may involve another person's legitimate decision.
It may reflect your own lack of preparation.
It may be the result of ordinary circumstances in a fallen world.
And sometimes, yes, genuine spiritual opposition may be involved.
But you cannot reliably identify the cause merely by observing that the door closed.
There are moments when God redirects.
There are moments when Satan opposes.
And there are moments when life is simply difficult.
Wisdom refuses to pretend that all three are the same thing.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that because you have been exhausting yourself fighting an enemy you have not actually identified.
You lost an opportunity, and you immediately assumed the devil stole it.
You experienced rejection, and you decided someone must have been attacking your future.
You encountered a delay, and you began questioning whether God had abandoned you.
But what if you stopped interpreting every painful event as a coded message and started bringing your circumstances honestly before the Lord?
What if you asked not only, "Why did this happen?" but also, "How can I honor Jesus in what happens next?"
Because you do not need to know the hidden reason behind every disappointment in order to remain faithful.
And you do not need a supernatural explanation for every closed door in order to trust God's sovereignty.
Now consider something even more unsettling.
Paul also wrote:
"For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries." — 1 Corinthians 16:9, KJV
Do you see it?
A great door was open.
And there were many adversaries.
The opportunity and the opposition existed at the same time.
If Paul had measured God's will only by how smoothly things were going, he could have mistaken the presence of adversaries for proof that the opportunity was wrong.
But he did not.
And this should challenge the way we speak about our lives.
Some Christians believe that if God is truly leading, everything will become easier.
Yet following Jesus has never carried a biblical guarantee of uninterrupted comfort.
Sometimes obedience costs money.
Sometimes integrity costs promotion.
Sometimes repentance costs relationships.
Sometimes telling the truth costs popularity.
Sometimes refusing compromise costs opportunities that would have made your life much easier.
And sometimes the right road is the road where you cry the most.
Not because God enjoys your suffering.
Not because pain automatically makes you holy.
But because faithfulness and comfort are not identical things.
Jesus Himself demonstrates this more clearly than anyone.
In the wilderness, the devil tempted Him with what appeared to be desirable outcomes.
In Matthew 4:8–10, Satan offered Jesus the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship.
Think about the nature of that temptation.
There was an offered path to worldly authority.
There was an apparent shortcut.
There was a proposed outcome that looked impressive.
But the price was disobedience to the Father.
Jesus did not evaluate the offer by its apparent benefits.
He answered with Scripture.
"Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve." — Matthew 4:10, KJV
That is discernment.
Not simply asking whether an opportunity is attractive.
Not simply asking whether it promises success.
But asking whether accepting it would require you to violate what God has already revealed.
An opportunity that requires disobedience is not made righteous by the rewards it promises.
And then we come to Gethsemane.
The place where simplistic ideas about God's will begin to collapse beneath the weight of the Gospel.
Jesus prayed in agony.
"O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." — Matthew 26:39, KJV
The road ahead was suffering.
Betrayal.
Humiliation.
The cross.
If pain alone meant someone was outside God's will, what would we do with Calvary?
If opposition always meant Satan had successfully closed the right door, how would we understand the suffering of the sinless Son of God?
Jesus was not outside the Father's redemptive purpose when He went to the cross.
He was obedient unto death.
Philippians 2:8 declares that Christ "became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross."
And through His death and resurrection, the salvation of sinners was accomplished.
The cross exposes the weakness of any theology that treats ease as the final measure of divine approval.
Because the greatest act of obedience in human history involved unimaginable suffering.
And the greatest victory was accomplished through what looked, to many watching, like devastating defeat.
There is something profoundly healing about that truth.
Because some of you have been judging your relationship with God by how much pain you have experienced.
You thought if God loved you, the marriage would have been easier.
You thought if God approved of your calling, the ministry would have grown faster.
You thought if you were truly faithful, people would have understood your intentions.
You thought if you prayed hard enough, every door you needed would eventually open.
And when life refused to cooperate, you started questioning yourself.
Maybe God is disappointed in me.
Maybe I missed my calling.
Maybe I am being punished.
Maybe I am not spiritual enough.
But hear this with the tenderness and seriousness it deserves.
A difficult season is not, by itself, a verdict on your standing before God.
Romans 8:1 says:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus."
Your acceptance before God is not purchased through perfectly interpreting circumstances.
It is grounded in Jesus Christ.
And if you belong to Him, you do not have to live terrified that one misunderstood opportunity has placed you permanently beyond His mercy.
That does not mean decisions are unimportant.
They matter deeply.
Some choices carry consequences that last for years.
Some require repentance, restitution, or the painful work of rebuilding trust.
But the Gospel is not the announcement that God only receives people who have always chosen correctly.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes yours.
Because maybe you did walk through the wrong door.
Maybe you ignored warnings.
Maybe you confused desire with direction.
Maybe you knew Scripture contradicted what you wanted, but you convinced yourself that your circumstances were an exception.
Maybe you called something a blessing because admitting the truth would have required surrender.
And now you are living with the consequences.
You feel ashamed.
You wonder whether you have ruined everything.
You replay the moment you should have turned around.
You wish you could go back and choose differently.
But the Gospel does not end with your worst decision.
The call of Christ is not to keep defending your mistake.
It is to repent.
To stop hiding.
To confess what is true.
To turn away from what dishonors Him.
To receive the mercy that only He can give.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say God forgives only those who misunderstood nothing.
It does not say grace is reserved for people who never followed the wrong opportunity.
It calls us to confession and rests our hope on God's faithfulness and righteousness.
And because Jesus died and rose again, forgiveness is not an empty religious wish.
It is rooted in the finished work of our Savior.
You may not be able to undo every consequence.
You may not be able to recover every lost opportunity.
You may need to make difficult changes.
But your failure does not have to become your final identity.
From scandal to grace is not the story of people who never fell. It is the testimony of sinners who discovered that Jesus Christ is greater than the sin that brought them to their knees.
And that brings us to a question every Christian should learn to ask before making a major decision.
Not merely, "Is the door open?"
But, "Is this faithful to Jesus?"
Does it contradict Scripture?
Am I being honest about my motives?
Am I seeking wisdom or simply looking for someone to approve what I have already decided?
Have I prayed with a willingness to accept an answer I do not prefer?
Have I listened to mature believers who know the Word and are willing to tell me the truth?
Am I overlooking a moral compromise because the opportunity is too attractive to lose?
Would I still believe this decision was right if it brought difficulty instead of immediate success?
These questions do not guarantee that every choice will become easy.
But they move us away from superstition and toward biblical wisdom.
Proverbs 3:5–6 teaches:
"Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths."
In Hebrew, the phrase translated "lean not" includes:
וְאֶל־בִּינָתְךָ אַל־תִּשָּׁעֵן
Ve'el-binatekha al-tishsha'en.
The instruction is not to rely upon your own understanding as though it were sufficient.
This is not a command to stop thinking.
It is a command to stop treating your limited perspective as ultimate.
And there is a profound difference.
God calls us to trust Him, not to abandon the wisdom He has given us through His Word.
James 1:5 tells believers who lack wisdom to ask God, who gives generously.
Romans 12:2 speaks of minds being renewed so that believers may discern God's will.
Hebrews 5:14 describes mature people whose powers of discernment have been trained through practice to distinguish good from evil.
And Psalm 119:105 declares:
"Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path."
A lamp.
Not a promise that you will receive a detailed explanation of every future event.
Not a guarantee that every circumstance will be immediately understandable.
But light sufficient to walk faithfully before God.
There will be decisions where Scripture gives a clear moral command.
Obey it, even if disobedience looks easier.
There will be decisions where several options are morally permissible.
Seek wisdom, consider your responsibilities, examine your motives, receive wise counsel, and choose responsibly.
There will be decisions where you genuinely do not know what will happen.
You can still act with humility and faith.
And there will be seasons where circumstances prevent you from doing what you hoped.
Grieve what you have lost if you need to.
Reconsider your plans.
But do not automatically accuse God of abandonment or Satan of interference.
You are not required to possess secret knowledge of heaven's every intention in order to live as a faithful disciple.
Deuteronomy 29:29 reminds us:
"The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law."
That is one of the most freeing truths you may ever embrace.
You are responsible to obey what God has revealed, not to decode everything He has kept hidden.
And perhaps the greatest danger of obsessing over doors is that we can become more fascinated with opportunities than with the One we claim to follow.
We want God to reveal which job will make us wealthy.
Which relationship will make us happy.
Which business will succeed.
Which move will change our lives.
Which decision will guarantee that we never experience regret.
But Jesus calls us into something deeper than the pursuit of favorable outcomes.
He calls us to Himself.
He says in Luke 9:23:
"If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me."
Not follow convenience.
Not follow every exciting opportunity.
Not follow every emotional impression.
And that is where genuine discernment begins.
With surrender.
Because sometimes the real issue is not that you cannot recognize God's will.
Sometimes the issue is that you are afraid of what obedience might cost.
You know what Scripture says about forgiveness, but you would rather hold on to bitterness.
You know what Scripture says about truthfulness, but the lie is protecting your reputation.
You know what Scripture says about sexual holiness, but the relationship makes you feel wanted.
You know what Scripture says about generosity, but your security has become attached to possessions.
You know what Scripture says about loving your enemies, but resentment feels justified.
And while you are waiting for another sign, the Word of God is already speaking.
Please do not mistake this for a call to reckless decisions or blind religious pressure.
Biblical obedience is not the same as accepting abuse, ignoring danger, neglecting your family, or surrendering your judgment to someone who claims to speak for God.
A pastor, ministry leader, partner, or spiritual adviser does not gain unquestionable authority over your decisions by saying, "God told me."
Test spiritual claims against Scripture.
Seek wise counsel.
Take real-world responsibilities seriously.
And remember that humility is not the enemy of faith.
It is one of the qualities faith should produce.
Perhaps right now you are standing in front of a decision that terrifies you.
You do not know whether to stay or leave.
You do not know whether to accept the offer.
You do not know whether the delay means anything.
You do not know whether the opportunity will succeed.
And you have been begging God for a certainty He has not promised to give you.
What if, instead of demanding to see the entire road, you began with the next faithful step?
Tell the truth.
Refuse the sin.
Seek counsel.
Fulfill your responsibilities.
Pray honestly.
Study Scripture carefully.
And where God has given freedom, make a thoughtful decision without pretending you have received an infallible revelation.
You may still experience disappointment.
You may still have to adjust your plans.
But you can trust that the God who saved you through Christ is not dependent upon your ability to interpret every circumstance perfectly.
Romans 8:28 speaks of God working all things together for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
And the following verse identifies the profound direction of that purpose: conformity to the image of His Son.
That means God's work in your life is bigger than getting you through the most profitable door.
Bigger than securing the most comfortable future.
Bigger than giving you the life you once imagined.
His purpose includes making you more like Jesus.
And sometimes that transformation happens through blessings.
Sometimes through correction.
Sometimes through waiting.
Sometimes through suffering.
And sometimes through the humbling discovery that what you desperately wanted was not nearly as important as the Savior you needed.
So before you celebrate the next open door, examine it.
Before you condemn the next closed door, be patient.
Before you tell someone that God must be blessing their decision because they are succeeding, remember Jonah's ship.
Before you tell someone that they must be outside God's will because they are suffering, remember Paul's adversaries.
And before you assume that the absence of pain is proof of divine approval, remember the cross.
The Gospel is not about finding a life where every door opens.
It is about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ, who died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
That is the hope beneath every decision.
That is the foundation beneath every disappointment.
That is the grace that meets us when our discernment has failed.
And that is why you must never allow the condition of a door to become more authoritative than the Word of the living God.
If this article has exposed a decision you have been wrestling with, I want to invite you into a moment of spiritual honesty.
Not performance.
Not pretending.
Just honesty before the Lord.
Maybe you need to say, "Jesus, forgive me for calling my desires Your direction."
Maybe your prayer is, "Lord, teach me to obey even when the road is difficult."
Maybe you are simply exhausted from trying to interpret every setback, and your heart needs to say, "Father, I trust You even when I do not understand."
You do not owe strangers the details of your private struggle. But your honest words may help another believer realize they are not the only one learning how to trust God.
It is good news for sinners who need a Savior.
That is also why we continue building Gospel Warrior as a place where believers can return for spiritual nourishment, biblical learning, encouragement, and resources that point them back to Jesus.
And you should never feel that you must pay money to prove your love for God.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
But the deepest reason to partner with a ministry should never be a discount.
It should be the desire to see Christ proclaimed, Scripture understood, believers strengthened, and people pointed toward the grace that transforms lives.
Our hope is in Jesus Christ alone.
If you are able to support, thank you. If you cannot, you are still welcome here, and the truth of God's Word remains worth sharing freely.
Because this mission has never been about selling access to God's love.
It is about proclaiming the Savior who loved us when we could never have earned His mercy.
And before you leave, I want you to remember one last thing.
One day you may look back at a door that never opened and realize you did not need everything behind it.
You may look back at an opportunity you walked away from and thank God that obedience mattered more than temporary success.
You may even look back at a painful mistake and marvel that the mercy of Jesus met you in the consequences.
But do not wait until you understand every chapter of your story before you trust the Author of your salvation.
The same Jesus who called sinners to repentance, welcomed the brokenhearted, forgave the guilty, and rose victorious from the grave is worthy of your trust today.
Not because every circumstance makes sense.
Not because every prayer receives the answer you expected.
Not because every door opens when you knock.
But because His character is faithful, His Word is true, and His saving grace is greater than your ability to predict tomorrow.
You may never understand why every door opened or closed—but you can know the Savior who is worthy of your trust on either side of it.
